title: Government budgets: deficits, surpluses and debt

explain.say: Think of a family planning the month: money in from jobs, money out for food and rent. Governments do the same, just with billions. Look at the board: government spending on one side, tax income on the other. They balance: a balanced budget.

draw.text: Government budgets: deficits, surpluses and debt

explain.say: Now spending grows heavier: new hospitals, roads and pensions. When spending is more than income, the gap is called a deficit. Many countries, from India to the USA, run deficits most years. What could a government do about the gap?

Look what fills the gap: borrowing. Governments sell bonds, which are IOUs, promises to pay back later with interest. Add up all the borrowing over the years and you get the national debt. Can you see the seesaw level again?
Sometimes tax income is heavier: that is a surplus, money left over. Oil-rich Norway saves its surpluses in a fund now worth more than 1.5 trillion US dollars. What would you do with a surplus?

Is borrowing good or bad? Look at both views. Followers of John Maynard Keynes say borrow to help in hard times; others warn big debts mean big interest bills. You thought like a finance minister! Wow: Japan's government debt is more than twice the size of its whole economy.

draw.name: x-compare
draw.verdict: Economists disagree on the right level

faq.a: A budget deficit is when a government spends more than it collects in taxes and other income in a year. It usually borrows to cover the gap.
A budget surplus is when a government collects more than it spends in a year. It can save the extra or pay off debt.
National debt is the total a government owes from all its past borrowing that has not been paid back yet.
asks: How much does a country owe?

faq.a: A bond is an IOU: you lend the government money, and it promises to pay you interest and return the money on a set date. Pension funds, banks and ordinary savers buy them.

It depends. Borrowing for useful things like roads, schools or fighting a recession can pay off. But very high debt means big interest payments and can scare lenders. Economists disagree about how much is too much.
asks: How much debt is too much?

facts: Norway's Government Pension Fund Global, built from oil revenues, is worth more than 1.5 trillion US dollars.
Japan's government debt is more than 200 percent of its GDP, among the highest in the world.
